stimuli.text: The temperature of a liquid, in degrees Celsius, is modeled by a differentiable function $$H$$ of time $$t$$, in minutes. Selected values are shown.
The graph of the function $$f$$ shown consists of line segments on $$0 \leq x \leq 6$$.

image.alt: Graph of f: line segments through the points (0, 1), (1, -1), (2, -1), (3, -3), (4, -3), (5, 2), (6, 1).

stimuli.text: Water enters a tank at a rate modeled by $$E(t) = 13 + 3\sin\left(\frac{t}{3}\right)$$ gallons per hour and leaves the tank at a rate modeled by $$L(t) = 5\sqrt{t + 1}$$ gallons per hour, for $$0 \leq t \leq 8$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the tank contains 61 gallons of water.

A particle moves in the xy-plane so that for $$0 \leq t \leq 3$$, $$\frac{dx}{dt} = 3\sin\left(\frac{t^2}{5}\right) + 1$$ and $$\frac{dy}{dt} = \cos(t)\,e^{t/4}$$. At $$t = 0$$ the particle is at $$(-2, 1)$$.
Consider the curve given by $$x^2 - xy + y^2 = 3$$.
A particle moves along the x-axis with velocity $$v(t) = 3t^{2} - 24t + 36$$ for $$t \geq 0$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the particle is at $$x = 0$$.
Consider the differential equation $$\frac{dy}{dx} = 4x(y - 2)$$. Let $$y = f(x)$$ be the particular solution with $$f(1) = 5$$.
A function $$f$$ has derivatives of all orders. Selected values are $$f(3) = -3$$, $$f'(3) = -1$$, $$f''(3) = -4$$ and $$f'''(3) = -12$$. For all $$x$$, $$|f^{(4)}(x)| \leq 12$$.

questions.stem: What is the average rate of change of $$H$$ over the interval $$2 \leq t \leq 7$$, in degrees Celsius per minute?

options.why: This is the average temperature, not the average rate of change.
This is the total change in temperature; it still needs to be divided by the elapsed time.
This divides time by temperature, which is upside down.

questions.explanation: Average rate of change $$= \frac{H(7) - H(2)}{7 - 2} = \frac{18 - 31}{5} = -\frac{13}{5}$$ degrees per minute.

questions.stem: A particle has velocity $$\vec{v}(t) = \langle 2t, 3t^{2} + 1 \rangle$$ and position $$(-3, -5)$$ at $$t = 0$$. Where is the particle at $$t = 3$$?

options.why: This is the velocity at the final time, not the position.
This is the displacement; add the starting position.
This adds the final velocity instead of the accumulated change in position.
Correct. Add the integral of each velocity component to the starting coordinate.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3} + h\right) - \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)}{h}$$?

options.why: Correct. The limit is the derivative of $$\sin x$$ at $$\frac{\pi}{3}$$.
This is the function value at the point, not the derivative.
Sign error: $$\frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x$$ and $$\frac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x$$.
Substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, an indeterminate form.

questions.explanation: The expression is the definition of $$f'\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)$$ for $$f(x) = \sin x$$, which equals $$\frac{1}{2}$$.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = 2x^{3} + 6x^{2} - 18x$$. At what value of $$x$$ does $$f$$ have a relative minimum?

options.why: $$f(0) = 0$$, but $$f'(0)$$ is not zero, so this is not a critical point.
At this critical point $$f'$$ changes from positive to negative, which gives a relative maximum.
This is where f″ = 0 (the inflection point), not a critical point.
Correct. $$f'(x) = 6(x + 3)(x - 1)$$ changes from negative to positive at $$x = 1$$.

questions.explanation: $$f'(x) = 6x^2 + 12x - 18 = 6(x + 3)(x - 1)$$. Testing signs: $$f'$$ is positive left of $$-3$$, negative between $$-3$$ and $$1$$, positive right of $$1$$. So there is a relative maximum at $$-3$$ and a relative minimum at $$1$$.

questions.stem: If $$\int_0^{1} f(x)\,dx = 9$$ and $$\int_0^{4} f(x)\,dx = -2$$, what is $$\int_{1}^{4} \left(-2f(x) + 4\right)dx$$?

options.why: This forgets to multiply the integral of $$f$$ by $$-2$$.
The integral of the constant $$4$$ over an interval of length $$3$$ is $$12$$, not $$4$$.
This adds the two given integrals; the integral from a to b is their difference.

questions.explanation: $$\int_{1}^{4} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^{4} f - \int_0^{1} f = -11$$. By linearity, the requested integral is $$-2 \cdot (-11) + 4 \cdot 3 = 34$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{3x^{3} - 1}{5x^{2} + 3}$$?

options.why: The limit is 0 only when the denominator has the higher degree.
Correct. The numerator has the higher degree and positive leading coefficients, so the outputs grow without bound.
This is the ratio of the constant terms, which only matters as x approaches 0.
Comparing leading coefficients only gives the limit when the degrees are equal.

questions.explanation: For large $$x$$ the expression behaves like $$\frac{3x^3}{5x^2} = \frac{3}{5}x$$, which grows without bound.

questions.stem: A particle moves along the x-axis so that its position at time $$t \geq 0$$ is $$x(t) = t^{3} - 18t^{2} + 96t$$. At what times is the particle at rest?

options.why: This is where the position is zero, not the velocity.
At $$t = 0$$ the position is 0, but the velocity is $$96$$, so the particle is moving.
This is where the acceleration is zero, not the velocity.
Correct. $$v(t) = 3t^2 - 36t + 96 = 3(t - 4)(t - 8)$$, which is zero at $$t = 4$$ and $$t = 8$$.

questions.explanation: The particle is at rest when $$v(t) = x'(t) = 0$$. $$v(t) = 3(t - 4)(t - 8)$$, so $$t = 4$$ and $$t = 8$$.

questions.stem: What is the sum of $$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} -2\left(-\frac{3}{5}\right)^n$$?

options.why: Correct. Geometric with first term $$-2$$ and ratio $$-\frac{3}{5}$$.
This divides by $$r$$ instead of $$1 - r$$.
The first term depends on the starting index; check the term for the first value of n.
The formula is $$\frac{a}{1 - r}$$, not $$\frac{a}{1 + r}$$.

questions.explanation: $$|r| = \left|-\frac{3}{5}\right| < 1$$, so the series converges to $$\frac{-2}{1 - \left(-\frac{3}{5}\right)} = -\frac{5}{4}$$.

questions.stem: Let $$g(x) = \int_0^{x} f(t)\,dt$$. What is $$g(4)$$?

options.why: Correct. $$g(4)$$ is the signed area from 0 to $$4$$.
Sign error: area above the axis counts positive.
This counts area below the axis as positive.

questions.explanation: $$g(4) = \int_0^{4} f(t)\,dt$$, the area above the axis minus the area below it on $$[0, 4]$$, which is $$-6$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\int_0^{3} \frac{1}{x + 3}\,dx$$?

options.why: This forgets to subtract the value at the lower limit.
Correct. $$\ln|x + 3|\Big|_0^{3} = \ln 6 - \ln 3 = \ln 2$$.
This uses a power-rule-style antiderivative; the antiderivative of 1/u is ln|u|.
This is the ratio minus one, not a logarithm.

questions.explanation: $$\int \frac{dx}{x + 3} = \ln|x + 3| + C$$, so the integral is $$\ln\frac{6}{3} = \ln 2$$.

questions.stem: Let $$C(x)$$ be the cost, in dollars, of producing x items. Which of the following is the best interpretation of $$C'(9) = 7$$?

options.text: The cost changes by 7 over the first 9 items.
options.why: This describes a total change over an interval, which is an integral of the rate, not the derivative at one point.

options.text: The average rate of change of the cost over the first 9 items is 7 dollars per item.
options.why: The derivative is an instantaneous rate at one input, not an average over an interval.

options.text: The cost when 9 items have been produced is 7.
options.why: This describes $$C(9)$$, the value of the function, not its rate of change.

options.text: The cost is increasing at a rate of 7 dollars per item when 9 items have been produced.
options.why: Correct. A derivative at a point is an instantaneous rate of change, with units of output per unit of input.

questions.explanation: $$C'(9)$$ is the instantaneous rate of change of $$C$$ when 9 items have been produced. Its sign (positive) says the cost is increasing, and its units are dollars per item.

questions.stem: Let $$y = f(x)$$ be the solution to $$\frac{dy}{dx} = x^2 - y$$ passing through the point $$(1, -2)$$. What is $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$$ at that point?

options.why: Sign error: the derivative of −y is −dy/dx.
Correct. $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 2x - \frac{dy}{dx}$$, and $$\frac{dy}{dx} = 3$$ at the point.
This differentiates x² but treats y as a constant; y depends on x.
This is dy/dx, the first derivative.

questions.explanation: Differentiate implicitly: $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 2x - \frac{dy}{dx} = 2x - (x^2 - y)$$. At $$(1, -2)$$: $$2 - 3 = -1$$.

questions.stem: A function $$f$$ has $$f(2) = -1$$, $$f'(2) = 2$$ and $$f''(2) = 6$$. Using the second-degree Taylor polynomial for $$f$$ about $$x = 2$$, what is the approximation of $$f(2.1)$$?

options.why: This forgets to divide the second derivative by $$2!$$.
This is the tangent-line (first-degree) approximation.
The quadratic term must use $$(x - a)^2$$, not $$(x - a)$$.

questions.stem: The sum of $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$$ is approximated by its first 6 terms. What is the smallest upper bound on the error given by the alternating series error bound?

options.why: This skips a term: the bound is the very next term.
This is the last term used, not the first one omitted.
Correct. The error is at most the first omitted term.
The exponent stays the same as in the series.

questions.explanation: The terms alternate, decrease in size and approach 0, so $$|S - S_{6}| \leq b_{7} = \frac{1}{7}$$.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n}{n + 1}$$?

options.why: Not this one: terms approach 1, not 0 (nth term test).
Not this one: terms approach 1, not 0 (nth term test).

options.text: It converges, but to a negative sum only if the first term is negative.
options.why: This statement is not a classification of convergence.
Correct. terms approach 1, not 0 (nth term test).

questions.explanation: Test the absolute values first, then the series itself: terms approach 1, not 0 (nth term test).

questions.stem: For the curve $$x^2 + xy + y^2 = 13$$, what is $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ at the point $$(-1, -3)$$?

options.why: Correct. $$2x + y + x\frac{dy}{dx} + 2y\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$$, so $$\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{2x + y}{x + 2y}$$.
This ignores the $$xy$$ term entirely.
Sign error when solving for dy/dx.
This differentiates $$xy$$ as $$y$$, forgetting the product rule term $$x\frac{dy}{dx}$$.

questions.explanation: Implicit differentiation with the product rule on $$xy$$: $$2x + (y + xy') + 2yy' = 0$$. Solving, $$y' = -\frac{2x + y}{x + 2y}$$; at $$(-1, -3)$$, $$y' = -\frac{5}{7}$$.

options.why: This leaves out the derivative of the upper limit, $$2x^{1}$$.
This evaluates the integrand at both limits; the derivative of an accumulation function only uses the variable limit.
The integrand must be evaluated at the upper limit, not at x.
Correct. By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus with the chain rule, substitute the upper limit and multiply by its derivative.

questions.stem: A particle moves along a line with velocity $$v(t) = t^{2} - t$$. What is the total distance traveled by the particle from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 2$$?

options.why: This is the velocity at the final time.
This is the displacement; it subtracts the distance traveled backward.
Correct. Total distance is $$\int_0^{2} |v(t)|\,dt$$; split at $$t = 1$$, where $$v$$ changes sign.
This counts the backward part twice.

questions.explanation: $$\int_0^{1} -v\,dt = \frac{1}{6}$$ and $$\int_{1}^{2} v\,dt = \frac{5}{6}$$. Total distance $$= 1$$.

questions.stem: The base of a solid is the region bounded by $$y = \sqrt{x}$$, the x-axis, and $$x = 2$$. Cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are isosceles right triangles with a leg in the base. What is the volume of the solid?

options.why: This is the volume for cross sections that are squares.
Correct. Each cross section has leg $$\sqrt{x}$$, area $$\frac{1}{2}x$$; integrate from 0 to 2.
This is the volume for cross sections that are semicircles.
This is the volume for cross sections that are equilateral triangles.

questions.explanation: The cross section at $x$ has leg $$\sqrt{x}$$, area $$\frac{1}{2}x$$. Integrating from 0 to 2 gives $1$.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the solution to $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x}{y}$$ with $$y(0) = 3$$?

options.why: The initial value is positive, so the positive root is needed.
This would have dy/dx = 1, which is not x/y.
Correct. $$y\,dy = x\,dx$$ gives $$y^2 = x^2 + C$$; $$C = 9$$, and the positive root matches $$y(0) = 3$$.
At $$x = 0$$ this gives $$\sqrt{3}$$, not $$3$$: the constant must be $$3^2$$.

questions.explanation: Separate: $$\int y\,dy = \int x\,dx$$, so $$\frac{y^2}{2} = \frac{x^2}{2} + C$$. With $$y(0) = 3$$, $$y^2 = x^2 + 9$$ and $$y = \sqrt{x^2 + 9}$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{x + 16} - 4}{x}$$?

options.why: This forgets that the conjugate denominator is $$\sqrt{x + 16} + 4$$, which approaches $$8$$, not $$4$$.
The expression is undefined at 0, but rationalizing shows the outputs approach a single number.
Substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, an indeterminate form.
Correct. Rationalizing gives $$\frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 16} + 4}$$, which approaches $$\frac{1}{8}$$.

questions.explanation: Multiply by $$\frac{\sqrt{x + 16} + 4}{\sqrt{x + 16} + 4}$$. The numerator becomes $$x$$, which cancels, leaving $$\frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 16} + 4} \to \frac{1}{8}$$.

questions.stem: What is the absolute maximum value of $$f(x) = x^{3} - 27x$$ on the closed interval $$[-5, 5]$$?

options.why: Correct. Compare $$f$$ at the critical points $$x = \pm 3$$ and the endpoints: the largest value is $$54$$.
This is a candidate value, but not the largest one. Check every critical point and both endpoints.
This is the absolute minimum value.
This is a candidate value, but not the largest one. Check every critical point and both endpoints.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = x^{3} + 5x - 5$$, and let $$g$$ be the inverse function of $$f$$. What is $$g'(13)$$?

options.why: This takes the reciprocal of a function value, not of the derivative.
This evaluates $$f'$$ at $$13$$ instead of at the input $$2$$ with $$f(2) = 13$$.
This is $$f'(2)$$; the inverse's derivative is its reciprocal.

questions.stem: What is the interval of convergence of $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(x + 2)^n}{n\cdot 6^n}$$?

options.why: The endpoints are reversed: the right endpoint gives the divergent harmonic series.
The radius is 6, from the factor $$6^n$$.
The left endpoint gives $$\sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$$, which converges.
Correct. Ratio test gives $$|x + 2| < 6$$; the left endpoint gives an alternating harmonic series (converges), the right endpoint the harmonic series (diverges).

questions.explanation: Ratio: $$\left|\frac{(x + 2)^{n+1}}{(n + 1)6^{n+1}}\cdot\frac{n\,6^n}{(x + 2)^n}\right| \to \frac{|x + 2|}{6}$$, so $$|x + 2| < 6$$. At $$x = 4$$: $$\sum \frac{1}{n}$$ diverges. At $$x = -8$$: $$\sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$$ converges.

questions.stem: For the curve $$x = t^2$$, $$y = t^{3} + 3t$$, what is $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$$ at $$t = 2$$?

options.why: Correct. Differentiate $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ with respect to $$t$$, then divide by $$\frac{dx}{dt} = 2t$$.
This forgets to divide by $$\frac{dx}{dt}$$.
This divides $$y''(t)$$ by $$x''(t)$$, which is not the second derivative.
This is $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$, the first derivative.

questions.explanation: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3t^2 + 3}{2t} = \frac{3t}{2} + \frac{3}{2t}$$. Its $$t$$-derivative is $$\frac{3}{2} - \frac{3}{2t^2}$$, which is $$\frac{9}{8}$$ at $$t = 2$$. Dividing by $$2t = 4$$ gives $$\frac{9}{32}$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\int_0^{1} xe^{x}\,dx$$?

options.why: This drops the second term produced by integration by parts.
Correct. Integration by parts, then evaluate at both limits.
Sign error in the integration-by-parts formula.
This evaluates only part of the antiderivative or only one limit.

questions.explanation: Use integration by parts: $$\left[xe^x - e^x\right]_0^1 = 0 - (-1) = 1$$.

questions.stem: The derivative of a function $$f$$ is $$f'(x) = (x + 4)(x + 2)$$. On which intervals is $$f$$ increasing?

options.why: This misses $$x > -2$$, where both factors are positive.
This misses $$x < -4$$, where both factors are negative so f′ > 0.
Between the roots the factors have opposite signs, so f′ < 0 and f is decreasing.
Correct. $$f'(x) > 0$$ when both factors have the same sign: $$x < -4$$ or $$x > -2$$.

questions.explanation: $$f$$ increases where $$f'(x) > 0$$. A sign chart for $$(x + 4)(x + 2)$$ is positive, negative, positive across $$-4$$ and $$-2$$.

questions.stem: What is the coefficient of $$x^{5}$$ in the Maclaurin series for $$f(x) = \frac{1}{1 - 3x}$$?

options.why: Sign error: check the sign pattern of the series.
The coefficient is the ratio raised to the nth power.
Correct. Substitute into the known Maclaurin series.
The geometric series has no factorials.

questions.explanation: $$\frac{1}{1 - u} = \sum u^n$$ with $$u = 3x$$: the coefficient of $$x^{5}$$ is $$3^{5} = 243$$.

questions.stem: Let $$P_{4}(x)$$ be the degree-4 Taylor polynomial for $$f$$ about $$x = 1$$, and suppose $$|f^{(5)}(x)| \leq 12$$ for all $$x$$. What is the Lagrange error bound for $$|f(\frac{11}{10}) - P_{4}(\frac{11}{10})|$$?

options.why: This uses the degree n instead of n + 1 for the factorial and power.
The distance from the center must be raised to the power n + 1.
Correct. $$\frac{12}{5!}\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)^{5}$$.
This forgets to divide by $$(n + 1)!$$.

questions.stem: What is the slope of the line tangent to the polar curve $$r = 3 + \cos\theta$$ at $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$$?

options.why: Sign error in $$\frac{dx}{d\theta} = r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta$$.
Correct. $$\frac{dy}{d\theta} = -1$$ and $$\frac{dx}{d\theta} = -3$$.
This is $$\frac{dr}{d\theta}$$, which is not the slope.
This is $$\frac{dx/d\theta}{dy/d\theta}$$, upside down.

questions.explanation: With $$x = r\cos\theta$$ and $$y = r\sin\theta$$: at $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$$, $$r = 3$$ and $$r' = (-1)$$. So $$\frac{dy}{d\theta} = r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta = -1$$ and $$\frac{dx}{d\theta} = r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta = -3$$; the slope is $$\frac{1}{3}$$.

questions.stem: Let $$y = f(x)$$ be the solution to $$\frac{dy}{dx} = x + y$$ with $$f(-2) = -1$$. Using the tangent line at $$x = -2$$, what is the approximation of $$f(-1.9)$$?

options.why: This adds the slope without multiplying by the step 0.1.
Sign error in the step.
This is only the estimated change; add it to f(a).

questions.explanation: At $$(-2, -1)$$, $$\frac{dy}{dx} = -3$$. The tangent line gives $$f(-1.9) \approx -1 + (-3)(0.1) = -1.3$$.

questions.stem: What is the sum of $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} -2\left(-\frac{3}{5}\right)^n$$?

options.why: The first term depends on the starting index; check the term for the first value of n.
The formula is $$\frac{a}{1 - r}$$, not $$\frac{a}{1 + r}$$.
This divides by $$r$$ instead of $$1 - r$$.
Correct. Geometric with first term $$\frac{6}{5}$$ and ratio $$-\frac{3}{5}$$.

questions.explanation: $$|r| = \left|-\frac{3}{5}\right| < 1$$, so the series converges to $$\frac{\frac{6}{5}}{1 - \left(-\frac{3}{5}\right)} = \frac{3}{4}$$.

questions.stem: What is the value of $$\int_{0}^{1} \sqrt{1 + x^3}\,dx$$?

options.why: This is a single rectangle using the right endpoint, a rough estimate rather than the integral.
Correct. Use the calculator's numerical integration.
This integrates over only half of the interval.
This is the change in the integrand, not the integral.

questions.explanation: On a graphing calculator, $$\int_{0}^{1} \sqrt{1 + x^3}\,dx \approx 1.111$$.

questions.stem: What is the absolute maximum value of $$f(x) = xe^{-x/3} + \frac{\sin x}{4}$$ on the interval $$[0, 10]$$?

options.why: This is where the maximum occurs (the x-value), not the maximum value.
This evaluates f at the critical point of the first term alone; the sine term shifts the maximum.
This is the value at the right endpoint, which is not the largest.
Correct. Graph f on the calculator and find its maximum on the interval, checking the endpoints too.

questions.explanation: On the calculator, the maximum of $$f$$ on $$[0, 10]$$ occurs at $$x \approx 2.153$$, where $$f(x) \approx 1.259$$. The endpoint values are smaller.

questions.stem: A particle moves in the plane with $$x'(t) = 3\cos\left(\frac{t^2}{2}\right)$$ and $$y'(t) = e^{t/4}$$. What is the total distance the particle travels from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 1$$?

options.why: Correct. Integrate the speed $$\sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}$$.
This is the straight-line distance between the start and end points.
This adds the component displacements instead of integrating the speed.
This is the speed at the final time.

questions.stem: The temperature of a room, in degrees Fahrenheit, is modeled by $$H(t) = 72 + 15\sin\left(\frac{t}{8}\right)e^{-t/20}$$, where $$t$$ is measured in hours. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the temperature at $$t = 5$$, in degrees Fahrenheit per hour?

options.why: This is the temperature itself, not its rate of change.
Correct. The calculator's numerical derivative of $$H$$ at $$t = 5$$ gives 0.842; the temperature is increasing.
This multiplies the rate by the time, which is not a rate.
This is the average rate of change over $$0 \leq t \leq 5$$, not the instantaneous rate.

questions.explanation: The instantaneous rate of change is $$H'(5) \approx 0.842$$ degrees Fahrenheit per hour, from the calculator's numerical derivative.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = x^2 e^{-x}$$. What is the value of $$f'(2.5)$$?

options.why: Correct. Use the calculator's numerical derivative (or the correct rule) at the given input.
This is the derivative at $$x = 3.5$$, not at $$x = 2.5$$.
This is the function value, not the derivative.
This multiplies the derivatives of the factors instead of using the product rule.

questions.explanation: On a graphing calculator, evaluate $$\left.\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^2 e^{-x}\right)\right|_{x = 2.5} \approx -0.103$$.

options.why: The numerator is not the derivative of the denominator, so this is not a logarithm.
Correct. Completing the square: $$x^{2} - 6x + 10 = (x - 3)^2 + 1$$.
This divides by the derivative of the denominator, which is not a valid antiderivative.
Sign error when completing the square.

questions.stem: A particle moves along a line with velocity $$v(t) = 4\sin(t)\,e^{-t/6} + 0.3$$. What is the total distance the particle travels over $$0 \leq t \leq 4$$?

options.why: This is the speed at the final time.
Correct. $$\int_0^{4} |v(t)|\,dt$$ on the calculator.
This is the average speed, not the distance.
This is the displacement; backward motion subtracts from it.

questions.explanation: Total distance $$= \int_0^{4} |v(t)|\,dt \approx 7.668$$. The displacement $$\int_0^{4} v(t)\,dt \approx 6.650$$ is smaller because the particle moves backward part of the time.

questions.stem:
Which of the following series converge?

I. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n!}{3^n}$$

II. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{\sqrt{n}}$$

III. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n}{n^2 + 1}$$

options.why: Check each series with an appropriate test: I diverges, II converges, III diverges.
Check each series with an appropriate test: I diverges, II converges, III diverges.
Correct. I: diverges (ratio test gives L = ∞). II: converges (alternating series test, but p = 1/2 for the absolute values). III: diverges (limit comparison with the harmonic series).
Check each series with an appropriate test: I diverges, II converges, III diverges.

questions.explanation: Series I diverges: ratio test gives L = ∞. Series II converges: alternating series test, but p = 1/2 for the absolute values. Series III diverges: limit comparison with the harmonic series.

questions.stem: What is the area of the region enclosed by the graphs of $$y = 4\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)$$ and $$y = x^2 - 1$$?

options.why: This is the distance between the intersection points, not an area.
Correct. The curves meet at $$x \approx -1.847$$ and $$x \approx 1.847$$; integrate top minus bottom.
This adds the absolute values of the curves instead of subtracting.
This is the area under the top curve only.

questions.explanation: Store the intersection x-values from the calculator, then $$\int_{-1.847}^{1.847} \left(4\cos\frac{x}{2} - (x^2 - 1)\right)dx \approx 12.257$$.

questions.stem: What is the area of the region bounded by the polar curve $$r = 3 + 0.5\sin^2\theta + \frac{\cos 3\theta}{2}$$ and the rays $$\theta = 0$$ and $$\theta = \pi$$?

options.why: The radius must be squared.
This divides by $$\pi$$, which is not part of the formula.
Correct. $$\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\pi} r^2\,d\theta$$ on the calculator.
This leaves out the factor $$\frac{1}{2}$$.

questions.explanation: $$A = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\pi} \left(3 + 0.5\sin^2\theta + \frac{\cos 3\theta}{2}\right)^2 d\theta \approx 16.837$$.

questions.stem:
Which of the following series converge?

I. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n}{n + 1}$$

II. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \cos\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)$$

III. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$$

questions.stem: Sand is added to a pile at a rate modeled by $$R(t) = 28 + 4\sin\left(\frac{t}{5}\right)\sqrt{t + 1}$$ cubic feet per hour, for $$0 \leq t \leq 4$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the pile contains 199 cubic feet of sand. How much sand is in the pile at $$t = 4$$?

options.why: Correct. $$199 + \int_0^{4} R(t)\,dt$$.
This assumes the rate stays at R(T) for the whole time.
This is only the sand added; include the initial amount.
This adds the rate at one instant, not the accumulated amount.

questions.explanation: Amount = initial amount + accumulated change = $$199 + \int_0^{4} R(t)\,dt \approx 199 + 123.457 = 322.457$$ cubic feet.

questions.stem: What is the coefficient of $$x^{3}$$ in the Maclaurin series for $$f(x) = e^{2x}$$?

options.why: The denominator is $$n!$$, not $$n$$.
Correct. Substitute into the known Maclaurin series.
Sign error: check the sign pattern of the series.
The constant must be raised to the same power as x.

questions.explanation: Replace $$x$$ by $$2x$$ in the series for $$e^x$$: the $$x^{3}$$ term is $$\frac{(2x)^{3}}{3!}$$, so the coefficient is $$\frac{4}{3}$$.
